what: This is the Class A share of Zillow Group, which operates the largest residential property website in the United States. The company sells advertising and software to real estate agents, rental landlords and mortgage lenders; the website itself is free to buyers and renters. Class A and Class C shares represent the same business with different voting rights.
customers: Real estate agents buying buyer leads, landlords and property managers advertising rentals, mortgage lenders, and the consumers who browse listings without paying.
money: Premier Agent advertising, Showcase listings and new construction marketing.
Multifamily and single-family rental listing advertising.
Zillow Home Loans and related services.
moat: The company’s advantage is consumer habit: American home buyers open Zillow first, which obliges agents to advertise there. That audience has survived every attempt to buy it away, and the rentals marketplace is now assembling a similar default position in a market that was previously split across many listing sites.
risks: The Class A and Class C shares trade at slightly different prices for identical economics, and the Class A line is less liquid, which can widen the spread when the stock moves.
The trailing period shows a net loss of about $113.0M, and the shares trade at about 52 times EV/EBITDA.
CoStar is spending heavily on Homes.com to break Zillow’s hold on the audience, and has the resources to persist.
Existing home sale volumes have been near multi-decade lows, which caps the residential advertising business until mortgage rates fall.
Changes to how real estate commissions work, following industry litigation, could reshape how agents buy marketing.
opportunities: Revenue has recovered from $1.9B in 2023 to $2.6B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $2.9B, achieved while home sales stayed weak.
Free cash flow of $313.0M is far better than the reported loss, which is depressed by non-cash share-based compensation and amortisation.
Rentals advertising is growing much faster than the company average and addresses a large, fragmented market.
Cash of $1.3B against $457.0M of debt funds the competitive fight without dilution.
The six analysts who publish on this share class average a $35.50 target, about 30% above the current price.
watch: Which share class is cheaper on the day, and then the same operating questions as the Class C line: rentals growth and audience share against Homes.com.
view: Before anything else, understand what you are choosing between. Zillow’s Class A and Class C shares represent claims on exactly the same business and the same cash flows; the difference is voting rights and liquidity, and the Class C line attracts far more analyst coverage and trading volume. The two prices drift apart by small amounts. Where they do, the rational move is simply to buy whichever is cheaper on the day, because nothing about the underlying economics differs. If you are buying an operating thesis rather than a governance position, pay attention to the spread and nothing else about the class distinction.

The operating thesis itself is straightforward and genuinely good. This is a classifieds business whose entire value rests on consumer habit: Americans open Zillow first when they want to look at houses, which means agents must advertise there, which funds the product that keeps consumers coming. Fifteen years of that loop has produced an audience nobody has managed to buy away, including CoStar, which is currently spending extraordinary sums promoting Homes.com with an agent-friendly pitch. The evidence so far suggests it has not worked: Zillow grew revenue from $1.9 billion to $2.6 billion during a period when existing home sales were at generational lows and a well-funded rival was advertising against it relentlessly.

The part I think is underpriced is rentals. The residential advertising business is a cyclical bet on mortgage rates falling and frozen homeowners finally moving. Rentals is not cyclical in the same way: it is a large advertising market that was historically scattered across dozens of listing sites, and Zillow already has the traffic to consolidate it. That is potentially a second business of comparable eventual scale, and it is growing considerably faster than the reported company average suggests.

On valuation, be honest about what the numbers say. The $113 million net loss is mostly non-cash compensation and amortisation, so ignore it; $313 million of free cash flow against $1.3 billion of net cash is the real picture. But 52 times EV/EBITDA is a full price that already assumes both the housing recovery and the rentals build-out. You are buying quality, not value. The two things that decide the outcome are audience share against Homes.com and the rentals growth rate — and if both hold, the multiple compresses on its own as earnings catch up.
bull: Buy whichever class is cheaper, the audience holds, rentals compounds into a second business, and a housing recovery arrives on top.
bear: CoStar’s spending slowly erodes the consumer habit the whole model depends on while home sales stay frozen, with a 52 times EBITDA multiple and no cushion.
